summary: Pass 1 static triage of the original sample (PE32 GUI, 4 sections, imagebase 0x400000, entry 0x4018A0) identifies a heavily obfuscated runtime-decrypting loader stub. The visible stub loads devenum.dll via a byte-reconstructed WCHAR name, validates the loaded module is PE32, and walks a 50-deep linear daisy-chain of decoy wrapper functions before reaching a single XOR decryptor (sub_401DF8). The decryptor materializes a 1716-byte (0x6B4) executable blob into a runtime-dependent buffer. Ciphertext is present in the file at .text VA 0x402A47. The oversized writable .rdata (0x66f58) is zero-filled at rest and is a decoy/reserved region, not the payload. No network, injection, registry, or persistence APIs are reachable in the visible stub; real capabilities reside entirely in the decrypted blob and are indeterminate at this pass. Unpack/recovery is required; the next recovery target is the 1716-byte decrypted stub at 0x402A47 (OEP = its first decrypted dword), key 0x9A246A73, XOR transform with a runtime-dependent destination.

findings.title: Obfuscated dynamic module loading of devenum.dll (DirectShow EnumMoniker)
findings.description: The entry point 0x4018A0 reconstructs the WCHAR module name 'devenum.dll' byte-by-byte in .data at 0x46B100 ('devenum*dll' with the '*' mutated 0x2A -> 0x2E via 'add byte ptr [ecx],4'), then calls LoadLibraryW (0x4018C8) to obtain a loaded base used as a scratch context for subsequent wrapper dword-offset reads.
findings.reasoning: Direct disassembly of start (0x4018A0): lstrcatW(0,0) and CryptUninstallCancelRetrieval thunk are decoys; the WCHAR mutation and LoadLibraryW call are reachable from entry. The returned base is validated by reading OptionalHeader.Magic via e_lfanew and compared to PE32 magic (cmp al,10h), with an infinite loop at 0x4018E6 if the check fails.

evidence.observation: start: lstrcatW(0,0) decoy; BYTE1(v2)=((unsigned __int16)&unk_46B200>>8)-1; *((_BYTE*)v2+14)+=4; LoadLibraryW(v2); *(base+e_lfanwen+28) compared to 0x10; else infinite loop; then sub_401090().
WCHAR buffer at 0x46B100 contains 'd','e','v','e','n','u','m','*','d','l','l'; byte 14 (0x2A) incremented by 4 to 0x2E ('.') giving devenum.dll.

findings.title: PE32 integrity / magic gate with anti-tamper infinite loop
findings.description: After LoadLibraryW the stub reads OptionalHeader.Magic (via e_lfanew at +60 and +28) and branches: if the magic is not 0x10B (PE32) it enters an infinite loop at 0x4018E6. Reachable from entry.
findings.reasoning: Disassembly 0x4018D0-0x4018E6 shows mov cl,3Ch; mov ecx,[ecx]; mov ecx,[eax+ecx+1Ch]; cmp al,10h; jnz to an empty infinite loop.

evidence.observation: PE optional header magic compared to 0x10; failure path is an infinite while(1) loop at 0x4018E6.

findings.title: 50-deep linear wrapper call chain obfuscation
findings.description: From sub_401090 the stub calls 50 small wrapper functions in a linear daisy chain, each calling the next with dword-offset reads off the loaded module base and punctuated by decoy API calls and LoadLibraryA pointer walk-back loops. The real logic (sub_401DF8) is reached only after the chain.
findings.reasoning: Callgraph analysis of the 51-function image plus disassembly shows a linear chain terminating at sub_401DF8; several wrappers contain self-recursion/pointer-walk decoy loops that terminate when LoadLibraryA returns NULL.

evidence.observation: Linear chain of ~50 wrapper functions from 0x401090 terminating at sub_401DF8; decoy self-loop edges present in 4019CC/4014AC/401580/401780/401A54/402068/402240/402368/4021F4.

findings.title: Single XOR decryptor sub_401DF8 materializes a 1716-byte executable stub
findings.description: sub_401DF8 (0x401DF8) is the only real code reached by the wrapper chain. It runs a 0x6B4 (1716)-byte loop with XOR key 0x9A246A73, reading a source buffer and writing the decoded stub to a runtime-dependent destination pointer derived from a LoadLibraryW return value. The 1716 bytes of ciphertext are present in the file at .text VA 0x402A47.
findings.reasoning: Direct disassembly of 0x401DF8 shows: push 6B4h; key constant 9A246A73h; loop loc_401E5A with 'xor ecx,[edx]' then 'pop dword ptr [ebx+ecx*2]'; counter compared to 6B4h. The write destination is computed from [LoadLibraryW_return + 0x11C], i.e. runtime-dependent and unresolved statically. get_bytes at 0x402A47 returned 2a 3a 7c 72 8a 95 db 65 ... confirming ciphertext in the file.

evidence.observation: push 6B4h; mov esi,9A246A73h; loop: xor ecx,[edx]; pop [ebx+ecx*2]; add edi,4; cmp edi,6B4h; jnz. Reads source buffer and writes decoded output via runtime pointer.
Bytes at 0x402A47: 2a 3a 7c 72 8a 95 db 65 71 1d 7d cc 03 d0 82 4e ... (ciphertext present in file, not zeros).

limitations: The exact plaintext transform (src^key, (src^key)-1, alternating key negation) and the decryption destination are runtime-dependent because the write pointer derives from a LoadLibraryW return value (see fin-decryptor-dest-unknown). Static decryption of the raw file bytes with simple candidate transforms did not produce clean ASCII, indicating a stateful/runtime key schedule or destination. This is the primary unresolved item for the unpack stage.

findings.title: Decryptor destination address is runtime-dependent (unresolved)
findings.description: sub_401DF8 computes its plaintext write destination from the return value of LoadLibraryW and an offset 0x11C, which is NULL in the file-loaded state. The true buffer base can only be determined at runtime (or after memory forensics), so the post-decrypt payload location is not statically knowable.
findings.reasoning: Disassembly of 0x401E31-0x401E3C: call [LoadLibraryW]; xchg eax,[...]; pop [eax+11Ch]; mov edi,[eax+11Ch]. Since LoadLibraryW returns NULL for the invalid name used, the destination pointer cannot be resolved statically.

evidence.observation: Write destination = [LoadLibraryW_return + 0x11C]; return is NULL for the invalid module name in the file, so the address is unresolved statically.

limitations: Resolution requires dynamic tracing or memory dump; not determinable from static analysis alone.

findings.title: Oversized writable .rdata is zero-filled decoy/reserved region, not payload
findings.description: The .rdata section spans 0x4040A8-0x46B000 (~0x66f58 bytes) and is marked writable, but at rest it is almost entirely zero-filled (raw size 0x600). It is not an embedded payload buffer; it is likely reserved 'room' for a later-stage heap/blob or deliberate decoy volume to mislead analysts.
findings.reasoning: get_bytes/section analysis shows the .rdata raw data is only 0x600 bytes of actual content and the rest is zeros. No embedded MZ/PE or file signatures are present anywhere in the image.

evidence.observation: .rdata 0x4040A8-0x46B000 marked rw, raw size 0x600, remainder zero-filled at rest.

limitations: The runtime write into .rdata cannot be excluded from static analysis alone; a dynamic pass is required to confirm.

findings.title: Import surface is largely decoy; no network/injection/registry/persistence APIs reachable
findings.description: The 42-entry import table is dominated by USER32, KERNEL32 utility, CRYPTNET, and DESK. No VirtualAlloc, CreateRemoteThread, Reg*, URL/network, WriteProcessMemory, or shell-execution APIs are imported. Many imported APIs (SetEvent, ReleaseMutex, FindAtomA, GetKeyState, GetClipCursor, timing APIs) are called only with NULL/0 args as decoy noise.
findings.reasoning: imports_query returned exactly 42 entries; find_regex for network/injection/registry/shell signatures returned 0 matches; decompilation of the wrapper chain shows decoy calls with NULL args. Real capability therefore resides in the decrypted blob and is not visible in the stub.

evidence.observation: 42 IAT entries across KERNEL32 (20), USER32 (13), CRYPTNET (5), DESK (1); no VirtualAlloc/CreateRemoteThread/Reg*/URL/WriteProcessMemory.
Regex for URLs/VirtualAlloc/CreateRemoteThread/Reg*/URLDownloadToFile/WriteProcessMemory returned 0 matches; all 47 strings are import/section names.

limitations: Capability inference is limited to the visible stub; the decrypted blob may resolve and use these capabilities dynamically.

findings.title: Payload handoff occurs inside the decrypted blob; OEP is its first decrypted dword
findings.description: No direct jump/call/ret into the ciphertext region exists in the visible stub; control transfers into the decrypted stub live in the decrypted bytes themselves. The effective payload entry (OEP) is the first decrypted dword of the 1716-byte blob at 0x402A47.
findings.reasoning: The wrapper chain ends at sub_401DF8 and returns through the chain; there is no static transfer into 0x402A47-0x4030FA in the visible code. The blob's nature (position-independent shellcode vs another image) is undetermined until decrypted.

evidence.observation: No code/data cross-reference into the ciphertext region from the visible stub; transfer target lives in decrypted bytes.

limitations: Post-decrypt control flow is not statically observable; requires the unpack stage or dynamic tracing to confirm.

investigation_targets.recommended_action: In the unpack stage, breakpoint after sub_401DF8 completes, dump the decoded buffer, and record its address (destination is runtime-dependent).

investigation_targets.recommended_action: Trace sub_401DF8 in a debugger; record eax/[eax+0x11C] and the first write address.
investigation_targets.success_criteria: Concrete destination address confirmed and mapped to the recovered payload.

investigation_targets.recommended_action: After recovery, repeat fingerprint + execution-graph mapping on the decrypted blob.
investigation_targets.success_criteria: Capability findings recorded with evidence, or marked indeterminate with reasons.

limitations: The decryptor write destination is runtime-dependent and unresolved statically (sub_401DF8 derives it from a LoadLibraryW return value).

Static candidate decryption of the raw ciphertext bytes with simple XOR transforms did not yield clean ASCII, implying a stateful/runtime key schedule or a non-file-resident source; plaintext recovery requires the dynamic unpack stage.
Post-decrypt control flow and the blob format are not observable statically; the handoff target (OEP) is inferred, not confirmed.
All capability conclusions are limited to the visible stub; the decrypted blob may resolve imports dynamically and its behavior is indeterminate at this pass.
The oversized .rdata is inferred to be a decoy/reserved region; a dynamic pass is needed to confirm no runtime writes target it.

reasons: The stub is a runtime-decrypting loader: real logic and all capabilities live in a 1716-byte blob decrypted at runtime by sub_401DF8.
The visible import surface and strings are decoys with no real network/injection/registry capability.
Ciphertext is present in the file at .text 0x402A47, confirming an embedded encrypted payload stage.
Post-decrypt handoff (OEP) is only resolvable after the blob is materialized.
